subject: Business Models
title: The 2-5% Rule
description: A fast breakdown of The 2-5% Rule for builders.

hook.text: In freemium businesses, only 2-5% of users typically convert to paid plans. That means 95% never pay.

buildup.text: The math: you need massive free user bases to generate enough revenue from the small paying minority.

discovery.text: If 1 million users generate 30,000 paid subscribers at $10/month, that's $3.6 million/year. Scale matters.

twist.text: Some companies achieve 25%+ conversion. Slack converts about 30% of its active teams. Design matters more than scale.

climax.text: The 2-5% isn't a law—it's the average. Better products with smarter paywalls convert far more.

punchline.text: 95% freeload, 5% pay. Smart design can flip those numbers.

quiz.question: What is the typical conversion rate in freemium businesses?

details.summary: The 2-5% rule describes the typical freemium conversion rate where only 2 to 5% of free users ever become paying customers. This means 95-98% of users consume resources without generating direct revenue, requiring the paying minority to subsidize the vast free majority.
details.whyItMatters: The 2-5% rule reveals the fundamental economics challenge of freemium: a tiny fraction of users must generate enough revenue to cover costs for everyone..
takeaways: Only 2-5% of freemium users typically convert to paying customers
The paying minority must generate enough revenue to cover all users' costs
Conversion rates below 2% make most freemium models financially unviable

faq.question: What factors determine where a product falls within the 2-5% conversion range?
faq.answer: Products with strong daily engagement convert higher because habitual use builds dependency. Clear value gaps between free and paid tiers motivate upgrades. Products serving professional needs convert better than entertainment..

faq.question: Can freemium businesses succeed with conversion rates below 2%?
faq.answer: Only if the free user base is enormous and serving free users is nearly costless. A social network with a billion free users can profit from advertising even if paid conversion is under 1%. But for products with meaningful per-user costs, sub-2% conversion usually leads to unsustainable losses.
